name: Frisian
line: Speak your own language, go out in the wind, keep your stretch of the dike and say plainly what you mean.

quote.text: If it cannot be done the way it should, it must be done the way it can.
quote.source: As it net kin sa’t it moat, dan moat it mar sa’t it kin

quotes.text: Butter, bread and green cheese: whoever cannot say that is no true Frisian.
quotes.source: Bûter, brea en griene tsiis; wa’t dat net sizze kin, is gjin oprjochte Fries. By tradition the test he put to captured sailors, about 1515

quotes.text: We Frisians kneel only before God.
quotes.source: Said to have been his answer in 1555 when told to kneel to Philip II. A tradition, first recorded later
Leaver dea as slaef. Carved on the monument at Warns that marks the defeat of the Count of Holland in 1345

quotes.text: Who will not dike must leave.
quotes.source: Dy’t net dykje wol, moat wike. A landholder who failed to keep up his length of dike forfeited his land

quotes.text: God made the sea, the Frisian made the coast.
quotes.by: Latin saying of the North Sea coast

quotes.text: As long as the wind blows from the clouds and the world stands.
quotes.source: The formula for how long the Frisians were to remain free, from the medieval law texts; a common rendering

quotes.text: No men stand before the Germans in arms or in good faith.
quotes.by: The Frisian envoys Verritus and Malorix
quotes.source: On seating themselves among the senators in the theatre of Pompey at Rome, AD 58; Tacitus, Annals 13.54

words.usage: The language and the people. It is the closest living relative of English on the continent.
The province in the north of the Netherlands. Since 1997 the Frisian form has been its official name.
Literally father’s land. A Frisian away from home is said to live outside the province, om utens.
The language learned at home. Rather more than half the people of the province have Frisian as theirs.
The village, the neighbours and the feeling of doing things together. The chosen theme when Leeuwarden was a European Capital of Culture in 2018.
The Frisian freedom was the medieval condition of having no count or duke between the people and the distant emperor.
A hill of clay, turf and dung raised by hand above the tide. More than a thousand were built before there were dikes.
An earth wall against the sea. The first ring dikes date from about the year 1000.
The shallow Wadden Sea between the coast and the islands, which falls dry twice a day.
Lakes, canals and ditches cover a large part of the province. A regional water board is a wetterskip.
Built from the eighteenth century to carry peat, manure and potatoes over shallow water. A family lived in the tiny cabin.
Eleven days of racing each summer between fourteen old cargo barges, each sailing for a town or village.
Vaulting over a canal by climbing a long pole as it swings across. It began as the way to cross ditches when looking for eggs.
Two teams of three strike a small hard ball with a gloved hand on a grass field. One of the oldest ball games in Europe.
A skating race and tour of nearly two hundred kilometres over the canals between the eleven old towns, held only when the ice is thick enough.
On natural ice, with long strokes, hands behind the back and head down into the wind.
The words with which the chairman announced the Eleven Cities Tour in 1985. They are now said of anything long hoped for.

words.meaning: A leaf of the yellow water lily
words.usage: Seven red ones lie on the blue and white stripes of the Frisian flag, standing for the seven sea-lands of the Middle Ages.
The old type is called head-neck-rump: a house, a narrow link and a great barn in one line.
The fortified home of a leading family, built of brick when everything else was wood and clay.
The obligation of the nearest households to help at a birth, an illness and above all a death, when they lay out the body and carry the coffin.

words.meaning: An evening visit for a talk
words.usage: Calling on neighbours after supper, without an invitation, for coffee and conversation.
Honest, simple and without airs. What a Frisian hopes to be called.
The stiff head of the Frisian is proverbial. A stânfries is one who stands firm and will not be moved.
What you say to someone facing a hard job or a headwind.
A much used word that covers strange, striking and suspicious, according to tone.
The feeling of being at ease in good company.
The everyday greeting, at any hour.
Tank alone is thanks.
Goodbye.

practices.name: Speak your mother tongue
practices.instructions: Use the language you were raised in today, on purpose. If you have a home language, a dialect or an accent that you put away at work or in town, bring it out: greet people in it, think in it, ring someone who shares it. If you only have one language, speak it slowly and plainly, without borrowed jargon. The rule of this Onda is to speak your own language.
practices.why: Frisian, Frysk, is a recognised language spoken by about half a million people. Using the mother tongue, memmetaal, with pride is the heart of Frisian identity.
variations: Phone someone and speak in dialect.
Write a note in your home language.

practices.name: Out in the wind
practices.instructions: Go out for forty minutes whatever the weather. Dress for it. Find open ground or water if you can, and walk or cycle the first half straight into the wind, so that it carries you home. Keep a steady pace and do not stop for the rain. The rule of this Onda is to go out in all weathers. Turn back if conditions are dangerous.
practices.why: Friesland is flat and windy, and Frisians cycle and walk in all weathers. The wind is part of the landscape.
variations: Go out in the rain with a good coat.

practices.name: Rye bread and clove cheese
practices.instructions: Eat a Frisian breakfast of dark rye bread with butter and slices of nagelkaas, a hard Frisian cheese with cloves and cumin, and a cup of tea or coffee. Sit at a table and eat slowly. Add a slice of ginger cake if you like. Frisian farms produced cheese and rye for centuries.
practices.why: Nagelkaas, clove cheese, is a spiced cheese of Friesland, eaten on rye bread. It is hearty and sharp.
variations: Try any hard cheese with caraway.

practices.name: Say it plainly
practices.instructions: In every conversation today, say what you mean in plain words, kindly and without padding. Frisians have a saying: rjocht en sljocht, straight and simple. Avoid hints, hedges and flattery. If you have bad news, say it gently but clearly. If you agree, say yes; if you do not, say so. Notice how people respond.
practices.why: Rjocht en sljocht, straight and plain, is a Frisian ideal. Plain speech saves time and builds trust.
variations: Give a compliment without adding a but.

practices.name: Read the sky and the water
practices.instructions: Look at the sky and the nearest water for ten minutes. Watch the clouds, the wind and the surface of the water. Predict the next few hours of weather, then check at noon. The Frisians’ lives have depended on weather and tides for two thousand years, and their landscapes are wide, so the sky is huge.
practices.why: The flat Frisian landscape gives a huge sky, and sailors and farmers read it. Watching clouds for ten minutes is a rewarding habit.

practices.name: A Frisian word or two
practices.instructions: Learn two Frisian words or phrases today: goeie, hello; tige tank, thank you very much; oant sjen, see you; noflik, pleasant; mienskip, community. Say them aloud to practise the sounds, which are close to English and Dutch. Greet someone with them or write them on a card.
practices.why: Frisian is the closest living language to English, and many words are almost identical: butter and fish are bûter and fisk. A few words is a friendly start.
variations: Say bûter, brea en tsiis for butter, bread and cheese.
Say oant sjen to a friend.

practices.name: Keep your stretch of the dike
practices.instructions: Name one thing that protects more people than yourself and that only holds if everyone does their part: a shared stairwell, a team’s records, a street, a club, a family’s finances. Find your stretch of it. Spend twenty minutes checking and strengthening it. Mend what is weak before the storm. The rule of this Onda is to keep your stretch.
practices.why: The dikes of Friesland protect the land from the sea, and each landowner was once responsible for a stretch. The lesson is that the whole holds only if each part does.
variations: Fix a small problem in a shared place.

practices.name: Head down and go the distance
practices.instructions: Do thirty minutes of steady effort in the open air: skating if there is ice, otherwise a run, a row, a sail, a long ride or a game with a ball. Choose a distance a little further than is comfortable and finish it at an even pace, kop derfoar, head to the front. Warm up first and stop if anything hurts.
practices.why: Kop derfoar, head first, is the Frisian spirit of getting on with it. The Eleven Cities Tour on skates, over 200 kilometres, is its greatest test.
variations: Skate if the ice is safe.

practices.name: Do your neighbour duty
practices.instructions: Do a neighbour duty today: carry the shopping, bring in the post, clear the snow, lend a tool, help with a task. In Frisian villages, buorplicht, neighbour duty, was a binding custom: neighbours helped at births, weddings and funerals, and with the hay. Offer and do not wait to be asked. The rule of this Onda is to stand by your neighbours.
practices.why: Buorplicht is the Frisian duty of neighbours to help one another. It is the practical side of the community spirit, mienskip.
variations: Take a plate of food to a neighbour.

practices.name: A game of draughts
practices.instructions: Play a game of Frisian draughts, Frysk damjen, or ordinary draughts, with a friend. The Frisian version is played on a 10 by 10 board, with kings and big captures. Concentrate and shake hands at the end. Frisian draughts has been played since the 17th century, in cafés and homes.
practices.why: Frisian draughts, or Frysk damjen, is a distinctive variant played in Friesland. It is a favourite winter pastime.

practices.name: A ball game
practices.instructions: Play a ball game in the Frisian spirit: keatsen, a handball game of the Middle Ages, in which two teams hit a small ball with the hand across a field, or any simple handball. Use a tennis ball and your palm. Count points and play on grass. Finish with a handshake.
practices.why: Keatsen is the Frisian national ball game, played since the Middle Ages, with its championship at Franeker. It is quick, social and cheap.
variations: Hit a ball over a rope.

practices.name: Walk the dike
practices.instructions: Walk along a dike, canal bank, sea wall or any embankment for half an hour, looking out over the water on one side and the land on the other. Frisians walk the dike to see the sea and check on the land. Think of the people who built it. Stay on marked paths, and watch the weather and tides.
practices.why: Dikes are the Netherlands’ great engineering works, and the best viewpoints in a flat land. A walk along one gives both perspective and quiet.
variations: Look for birds on the water.

practices.name: An evening visit
practices.instructions: After supper, call on a neighbour or a friend nearby, or ask one in. Keep it simple: coffee or tea and something sweet, sitting at the kitchen table. Talk about what is going on in the street, the village, the family. Say little about yourself and listen a great deal. Leave when the talk falls quiet. The Frisian word is jûnpraten, evening talk.
practices.why: Evening visits were the heart of village life in Friesland, with neighbours dropping in for coffee and a chat. It is a custom that deserves reviving.

practices.name: East Frisian tea
practices.instructions: Make tea in the East Frisian way: put a lump of rock sugar, kluntje, in a cup and pour strong black tea over it, so that it crackles. Then pour a spoon of cream down the side so that it forms a cloud, wulkje. Do not stir. Sip three times, first cream, then tea, then sweetness. Do it slowly.
practices.why: East Frisian tea is a ritual of the German coast, drunk with kluntje and cream. It is a world apart from a tea bag at a desk.

practices.name: Listen to a Frisian song
practices.instructions: Play a song in Frisian, such as Nynke Laverman’s Sielesâlt, Twarres’s Wêr bisto or De Kast’s In nije dei, or the anthem De Alde Friezen. Listen to the sound of the language and follow a translation. Note how the words move. Music in Frisian is a way of keeping the language alive.
practices.why: Frisian pop and folk, from Nynke Laverman to De Kast, show a language alive and growing. A few songs are a good introduction.
variations: Share a song with a friend.

practices.name: A dike-builder’s tale
practices.instructions: Read a few pages of Theodor Storm’s 1888 novella of a dike-reeve fighting the sea on the North Frisian coast. Read slowly, by lamplight. It tells of a man who builds a new dike against old opposition and of the ghostly rider on the dike. Imagine the storm. Note the sense of the sea as a threat.
practices.why: Der Schimmelreiter is the great novella of the North Sea coast, a story of a dike-builder, progress and superstition. It is atmospheric and compelling.
variations: Look at a photo of the dike it describes.

practices.name: Stars over flat land
practices.instructions: Go outside after dark and look at the stars over the flat horizon. In Friesland the sky is vast and, away from towns, dark. Find the Plough and the Pole Star. Notice how many stars you can see from the flat ground. Stand for fifteen minutes. If you live in a city, go to a park or the edge of the town.
practices.why: The Wadden Sea region is one of the darkest in Western Europe and a great place to see stars. A flat horizon makes the night sky seem enormous.

practices.name: Cycle to the sunset
practices.instructions: Cycle or walk out to see the sunset, on a flat road, by a canal, on a dike or at the edge of town. Choose a spot with an open view. Stop when the sun touches the horizon and stay until it has gone. Frisians grew up under big skies, with long evenings. Ride home slowly with lights on.
practices.why: Evening cycling is a way of life in the Netherlands. A sunset ride under a big sky is a simple, satisfying end to the day.

practices.name: A day on the water
practices.instructions: Spend a day on the water in the Frisian manner: sail, row, paddle or take a ferry on a lake, river or canal. Frisians have sailed the meres for centuries in flat-bottomed skûtsjes. Take food and water, wear a life jacket and go with someone. Watch the sky and the wind. Come ashore tired and content.
practices.why: The Frisian lakes are a paradise for sailors, and skûtsjesilen, the annual race of traditional barges, is a national event. A day on the water is the best way to feel it.
variations: Take a ferry to an island.
Paddle a canoe along a canal.

practices.name: The long ride
practices.instructions: Take a long ride of two hours, by bike on flat roads or by skate if the ice is safe, in the spirit of the Eleven Cities Tour. Set a route to a distant village and a café, ride at an even pace and go home by another way. Dress for the wind and carry water. Reward yourself with coffee and a sweet.
practices.why: The Elfstedentocht, the Eleven Cities Tour, is a 200-kilometre skating race held only when the ice is thick enough. A long ride is the summer cousin.

immersePlan.name: Read The Rider on the White Horse
immersePlan.text: Read the opening chapters of Storm’s novella of a dike-builder on the North Frisian coast. Notice the weather.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Edge of the World
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Michael Pye’s history of the North Sea and its peoples, including the Frisians. Mark one surprising fact.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Comfort Bird
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Hylke Speerstra’s novel in translation, a Frisian story of a farm family. Notice the plain voice.

immersePlan.name: Watch De Hel van ’63
immersePlan.text: Watch Steven de Jong’s 2009 film about the legendary Eleven Cities Tour of 1963, when only 69 skaters finished. Feel the cold.

immersePlan.name: Watch Nynke
immersePlan.text: Watch Pieter Verhoeff’s 2001 Frisian-language film about a girl in a farming family. Notice the sound of Frisian.

immersePlan.name: Watch the 1997 Eleven Cities Tour
immersePlan.text: Watch the footage of the 1997 skating tour, the last held so far. Notice the crowds and the effort.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Sielesâlt
immersePlan.text: Play Nynke Laverman’s 2004 album, a blend of Frisian poetry and Mediterranean sounds. Follow a translation.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In nije dei
immersePlan.text: Play De Kast’s 1997 Frisian rock album. Notice how natural the language sounds in rock.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Wêr bisto
immersePlan.text: Play Twarres’s 2000 album of folk-rock in Frisian. Sing along to the chorus.

immersePlan.name: Look at Hindeloopen painted furniture
immersePlan.text: Look at the brightly painted chests and chairs of the little port of Hindeloopen, with red and blue flowers. Choose a pattern.

immersePlan.name: Look at Makkum earthenware
immersePlan.text: Look at the blue-and-white pottery of Makkum, made since the 16th century. Compare it with Delft.

immersePlan.name: Look at Jopie Huisman’s paintings
immersePlan.text: Look at the realistic paintings of old, worn objects by the Workum rag-and-bone man. Notice the dignity of a battered boot.

immersePlan.name: Bake sûkerbôle
immersePlan.text: Bake sugar bread, a rich yeast loaf with lumps of sugar and cinnamon. Eat a thick slice with butter.

immersePlan.name: Eat clove cheese on rye
immersePlan.text: Eat nagelkaas on dark rye bread with butter. If you cannot find it, use any hard cheese with caraway.

immersePlan.name: Bake dúmkes
immersePlan.text: Bake thumb-sized spiced biscuits and eat them with tea. They are a Frisian favourite.

immersePlan.name: Learn about Beerenburg
immersePlan.text: Beerenburg is a herbal bitter from Friesland, usually with gin. Read about it, and drink a cup of hot herbal tea with a spoon of honey instead.

immersePlan.name: Drink a small cup of coffee
immersePlan.text: Drink a small cup of coffee with a biscuit or sugar lump, as is the Frisian custom, and chat.

immersePlan.name: Make East Frisian tea
immersePlan.text: Pour strong tea over a lump of rock sugar and add a cloud of cream. Do not stir.

immersePlan.name: Do your neighbour duty
immersePlan.text: Do one favour for a neighbour without being asked, and be ready to do another.

immersePlan.name: Learn about Sint Piter
immersePlan.text: Sint Piter is the feast of 21 February in Grou, when children go round the village with singing and sweets. Sing a verse to a neighbour.

immersePlan.name: Light a bonfire of Biike, in spirit
immersePlan.text: On 21 February North Frisians light big bonfires at dusk and eat kale and sausage. Light a candle and eat a plate of kale in the same spirit.

immersePlan.name: Play keatsen
immersePlan.text: Play a handball game with a tennis ball and your palm. Count points on a grass court.

immersePlan.name: Play Frisian draughts
immersePlan.text: Play a game of draughts with a friend on a larger board if you have one.

immersePlan.name: Watch fierljeppen
immersePlan.text: Watch a video of fierljeppen, the Frisian sport of pole-vaulting across a canal. Do not try it unless trained. Jump a puddle instead.

immersePlan.name: Look up Skûtsjesilen
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the annual race of traditional flat-bottomed sailing barges on the Frisian lakes in July and August.

immersePlan.name: Look up Leeuwarden
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Ljouwert, the Frisian capital, with its leaning tower, canals and the birthplace of Mata Hari.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Wadden Sea
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the UNESCO-listed tidal flats and islands, one of the world’s great wetlands, and the walk across the mud at low tide, wadlopen.

immersePlan.name: Practise mienskip
immersePlan.text: Mienskip is community. Do one thing today that strengthens the community around you.

immersePlan.name: Practise kop derfoar
immersePlan.text: Kop derfoar means head first, get on with it. Do the thing you have been putting off, now.

immersePlan.name: Practise jûnpraten
immersePlan.text: Jûnpraten is the evening talk. Spend half an hour in easy talk with a neighbour or friend.

rules.why: Use it at home and in the street. A language lives only in the mouth.
Wind and rain are no reason to stay in. Head into it first.
The dike holds only if each part holds. See to yours without being told.
Be there at the birth, the sickbed and the grave.
Say what you mean in few words, and do not put on airs.

rules.text: Bow to no one, and get on with it
rules.why: Keep your freedom, keep your head down and finish the job.

read.title: The Rider on the White Horse
read.creator: Theodor Storm
read.why: Der Schimmelreiter. A gifted, proud dike master on the North Frisian coast builds a new kind of dike against the will of his village. The great novel of the sea wall.

read.title: Rimen en Teltsjes
read.creator: Joost, Eeltsje and Tsjalling Halbertsma
read.why: Rhymes and Tales. Songs, comic stories and poems by three brothers, the book that made Frisian a written language again. Every household had one.

read.title: Strange Shores
read.creator: Tsjêbbe Hettinga
read.why: Frjemde kusten. Long, rolling poems of sea, land and leaving by a blind poet who recited them from memory. Published with English translations.

read.title: The Comfort Bird
read.creator: Hylke Speerstra
read.why: De treastfûgel. Two Frisian families, one that emigrated to America and one that stayed, followed through a century and a world war.

read.title: The Edge of the World: How the North Sea Made Us
read.creator: Michael Pye
read.why: A history of the North Sea that opens with the Frisian traders who brought money and markets back to northern Europe.

read.title: The Riddle of the Sands
read.creator: Erskine Childers
read.why: Two Englishmen in a small yacht among the sandbanks and tides of the East Frisian islands. The first modern spy novel.

watch.title: De Hel van ’63
watch.creator: Steven de Jong
watch.why: The Eleven Cities Tour of 1963, the coldest and hardest ever skated, through four of those who set out.

watch.title: De Dream
watch.creator: Pieter Verhoeff
watch.why: A Frisian-language film about three poor brothers convicted of a burglary in 1895 on doubtful evidence, and the fight to clear them.

watch.title: Nynke
watch.creator: Pieter Verhoeff
watch.why: The marriage of the children’s writer Nienke van Hichtum and the socialist leader Pieter Jelles Troelstra. In Frisian and Dutch.

watch.title: The Eleven Cities Tour of 1997
watch.creator: Dutch public television
watch.why: The broadcast of the last race, from the start in the dark at Leeuwarden to the finish on the Bonkevaart.

listen.title: Sielesâlt
listen.creator: Nynke Laverman
listen.why: Salt of the soul. Poems translated into Frisian and sung in the style of Portuguese fado.

listen.title: Wêr bisto
listen.creator: Twarres
listen.why: Where are you. A song in Frisian by two teenagers that went to number one in the Netherlands and Flanders.

listen.title: In nije dei
listen.creator: De Kast
listen.why: A new day. A ballad from a Frisian-language rock musical that became a national hit.

listen.title: De Alde Friezen
listen.creator: Words by Eeltsje Halbertsma, 1829, revised 1875
listen.why: The Old Frisians, the anthem of the province, sung standing at every match and gathering.

art.title: Painted furniture of Hindeloopen
art.creator: The craftsmen of a small seafaring town
art.why: Cupboards, chairs and sledges covered in curling flowers and leaves in red, green and blue, in a style its sailors brought home.

art.title: Makkum earthenware
art.creator: Royal Tichelaar Makkum
art.why: Tin-glazed pottery and tiles made from local sea clay by a firm that has worked in the village for more than four hundred years.

art.title: The paintings of Jopie Huisman
art.creator: Jopie Huisman of Workum
art.why: A rag and scrap dealer who taught himself to paint the worn things he collected. His museum is in his home town.

art.title: The owl board
art.creator: Frisian farm builders
art.why: A carved board on the gable of a barn, with two swans back to back above the hole left for owls.

eat.title: Sûkerbôle
eat.creator: Sugar bread
eat.why: A white loaf baked with lumps of sugar and cinnamon. Traditionally given to a mother who has had a daughter.

eat.title: Clove cheese on rye
eat.creator: Nagelkaas with Frisian rye bread
eat.why: A firm skimmed-milk cheese spiced with cloves and cumin, on dark steamed rye.

eat.title: Oranjekoek
eat.creator: A pink-iced cake with almond paste
eat.why: Scented with candied orange peel and aniseed. Served at weddings and birthdays.

eat.title: Dúmkes
eat.creator: Thumb biscuits
eat.why: Small hard biscuits with hazelnut and aniseed, with the dent of the baker’s thumb in each.

drink.title: Beerenburg
drink.creator: A bitter of gin and herbs
drink.why: Made with a mixture of some fifteen herbs first sold in Amsterdam by Hendrik Beerenburg in the eighteenth century and taken up by Frisian skippers.

drink.title: Coffee
drink.creator: A small cup, often
drink.why: The drink of every visit, poured as soon as you sit down.

drink.title: East Frisian tea
drink.creator: Strong black tea over rock sugar, with cream
drink.why: Across the border in Germany the Frisians drink more tea per head than anyone. The cream is laid on with a spoon and never stirred, and three cups is the rule.

customs.title: Neighbour duty
customs.creator: Buorplicht
customs.why: The households on either side are told first of a death. They inform the village, lay out the body and carry the coffin.

customs.title: Sint Piter
customs.creator: 21 February, in Grou
customs.why: The village of Grou keeps its own bringer of gifts in place of Saint Nicholas: Saint Peter, in a white cloak, with his helper.

customs.title: Looking for lapwing eggs
customs.creator: Aaisykjen, in March
customs.why: Finding the first lapwing egg of the year was an honour. Taking eggs is now barred, and the searchers mark and protect the nests from the mowers.

customs.title: The fire of Biike
customs.creator: 21 February, North Frisia
customs.why: On the islands and coast of North Frisia great bonfires are lit at dusk to drive out the winter, followed by a supper of kale.

games.title: Keatsen
games.creator: Handball · Friesland
games.why: A server strikes the ball to the opposing three, who try to return it past a line. The main tournament, at Franeker, has been held each summer since 1854.

games.title: Fierljeppen
games.creator: Pole vaulting for distance · Friesland
games.why: The jumper sprints to a pole standing in the canal, climbs it as it tips forward and drops on a sand bed. The record is over twenty-two metres.

games.title: Skûtsjesilen
games.creator: Sailing · Friesland
games.why: Old iron cargo barges twenty metres long, sailed by crews of a dozen or more from the villages they once served.

games.title: Frysk damjen
games.creator: Draughts · Friesland
games.why: Draughts on a hundred squares in which pieces capture straight as well as diagonally, which makes the game sharp and fast.

games.title: The Eleven Cities Tour
games.creator: Skating · Friesland
games.why: Skaters collect a stamp in each of the eleven towns. Three hundred race and sixteen thousand follow as tourers.

festivals.title: Skûtsjesilen
festivals.creator: Late July and early August
festivals.why: Eleven race days on different lakes, followed by a fleet of spectator boats.

festivals.title: The PC at Franeker
festivals.creator: The fifth Wednesday after 30 June
festivals.why: The great day of keatsen, when the best player is named king and the winners are driven round in a carriage.

festivals.title: Sneek Week
festivals.creator: From the first Saturday of August
festivals.why: The largest inland sailing regatta in Europe, with a fair and fireworks in the town.

festivals.title: Oerol
festivals.creator: Ten days in June, Terschelling
festivals.why: A festival of theatre and music that uses the beaches, dunes and barns of a Wadden island as its stages.

places.title: Leeuwarden
places.creator: Ljouwert, Friesland
places.why: The capital, with the leaning tower called the Oldehove, which began to sink while it was being built in 1529, and the Fries Museum.

places.title: The Eise Eisinga Planetarium
places.creator: Franeker, Friesland
places.why: A working model of the solar system built into the living room ceiling of a wool comber between 1774 and 1781. It still runs. A World Heritage site.

places.title: The terp of Hegebeintum
places.creator: North of Leeuwarden
places.why: The highest dwelling mound in the country, nearly nine metres above sea level, with a small church on top. Much of it was dug away for fertile soil.

places.title: The Wadden Sea
places.creator: The coast and islands from Den Helder to Denmark
places.why: The largest unbroken system of tidal flats in the world, and a World Heritage site. Take the ferry to Schiermonnikoog or Terschelling.

places.title: The Wouda pumping station
places.creator: Lemmer, Friesland
places.why: The largest steam-driven pumping station ever built, opened in 1920 and still fired up when the water is high.

places.title: The Red Cliff
places.creator: Warns, Friesland
places.why: A low bluff on the old sea coast with the boulder that commemorates the battle of 1345. Frisians gather there each September.

ethics.title: Freedom
ethics.text: Kneel to no one. Decide your own affairs with your equals.
ethics.practice: Where are you bowing today when you need not?

ethics.title: Shared duty
ethics.text: Each keeps a part of what protects all.
ethics.practice: Do your part of a common task before you are asked.

ethics.title: Plain dealing
ethics.text: Say what you mean and do what you say.

ethics.title: Steadfastness
ethics.text: Do not give up because the wind is against you.
ethics.practice: Carry on with one thing for ten minutes past the point where you want to stop.

ethics.title: Neighbourliness
ethics.text: The nearest houses are your first family in need.
ethics.practice: Find out how the people next door are.

ethics.title: Loyalty to your own
ethics.text: Language, village and landscape are yours to keep.
ethics.practice: Use a word today that only people from your home would know.

philosophy.title: Freedom without a lord
philosophy.text: For some three centuries the Frisians had no count, no knights and no serfs. Farmers judged their own cases.
philosophy.practice: What in your life do you run without a boss, and how well?

philosophy.title: Freedom as shared burden
philosophy.text: That freedom was possible because everyone was bound to the dike. Liberty and duty came together.
philosophy.practice: What obligation makes your freedom possible?

philosophy.title: Land that is made
philosophy.text: Much of the country was won from the sea by hand and can be lost again.
philosophy.practice: What do you have that only lasts as long as you maintain it?

philosophy.title: A small language
philosophy.text: A tongue spoken by half a million people has no use except to those who love it.
philosophy.practice: What do you keep alive for no practical reason?

philosophy.title: Stubbornness
philosophy.text: The stiff head is a fault and a strength. It kept a people distinct for two thousand years.
philosophy.practice: Where is your stubbornness serving you, and where not?

philosophy.title: Plainness
philosophy.text: No show, no rank, few words.
philosophy.practice: What would be left of your day with the display taken out?

philosophy.title: Staying and leaving
philosophy.text: Many Frisians emigrated, and many who stayed speak of those outside the province as still belonging.
philosophy.practice: Where is home if you have left it?

philosophy.title: If not as it should, then as it can
philosophy.text: When the right way is closed, find a workable one and get on.
philosophy.practice: What are you not doing because you cannot do it perfectly?

intro: The Frisians are the people of the low coast of the North Sea. Roman writers of the first century already knew them by that name, living on the marshes between the Rhine and the Ems. Today there are three groups. By far the largest lives in Fryslân, a province in the north of the Netherlands with some 660,000 inhabitants, where West Frisian is spoken. Across the German border a few thousand speak Saterland Frisian and North Frisian, the latter on the coast and islands just below Denmark. East Frisia in Germany keeps the name and much of the identity, though its language is now Low German.

Their history has been shaped by water. The first settlers farmed salt marsh that flooded at every high tide, and from about 500 BC they raised mounds of clay and dung, called terpen, on which to build. The Roman writer Pliny described people of this coast living like sailors when the sea covered the land and like the shipwrecked when it withdrew. Around the year 1000 they began to link the mounds with dikes, and over the following centuries enclosed, drained and reclaimed the land they now live on. Keeping the dikes was a shared duty laid down in law, and whoever could not maintain his length lost his farm.

In the early Middle Ages the Frisians were the great traders of northern Europe, carrying cloth, slaves and wine between the Rhineland, England and Scandinavia. Their kings, the best remembered of whom is Redbad, resisted both the Franks and Christianity until a defeat in 734. Later, uniquely in Europe, feudalism never took hold. From the eleventh century to the end of the fifteenth the Frisian lands had no count and no nobility with rights over the farmers, who governed themselves through assemblies and their own written laws. This was the Frisian freedom, and its memory is still the centre of Frisian identity.

It ended in 1498, and Friesland later became one of the seven provinces of the Dutch Republic. Frisian ceased to be used in government and was for three centuries a spoken language only. It was revived as a literary language in the nineteenth century by writers such as the Halbertsma brothers. In the twentieth century a language movement won its use in court, in schools and in the provincial government, and it is now the second official language of the Netherlands.

Frisian is the closest relative of English. A rhyme makes the point: butter, bread and green cheese is good English and good Frisian. Otherwise the culture is known for black horses and black-and-white cattle, for sailing and for skating, above all the Eleven Cities Tour, which can be held only in the rare winters when two hundred kilometres of canal freeze hard.
Frisians have a reputation among the Dutch for being stubborn, taciturn, proud and direct. They tend to agree, and take it as praise.
This Onda takes its practices from that life: the mother tongue, the wind, the stretch of dike, the long distance and the evening visit.
guide.origin: The North Sea coast, from the north of the Netherlands across north-west Germany to the Danish border
guide.era: Farmers settled the salt marshes about 600 BC. Around half a million people speak a Frisian language now

figures.name: Redbad
figures.bio: King of the Frisians, who fought the Franks and won back his kingdom. Legend says he stepped back from the baptismal font on being told his ancestors were in hell, preferring their company.

figures.name: Grutte Pier
figures.bio: Pier Gerlofs Donia, a farmer of great size who turned rebel and pirate after soldiers burned his village. His seven-foot sword is in the Fries Museum.

figures.name: Menno Simons
figures.bio: A village priest from Witmarsum who left the church in 1536 and led the peaceful Anabaptists. The Mennonites are named after him.

figures.name: Gysbert Japicx
figures.bio: A schoolmaster of Bolsward who wrote poetry in Frisian when no one else did. The chief Frisian literary prize bears his name.

figures.name: Maria Louise of Hesse-Kassel
figures.bio: Princess and twice regent, who lived simply in Leeuwarden and was loved as Marijke Meu, Aunt Mary. Every reigning monarch in Europe descends from her.

figures.name: Eise Eisinga
figures.bio: A wool comber of Franeker who taught himself mathematics and built a planetarium in his house to calm fears of a collision of the planets.

figures.name: The Halbertsma brothers
figures.bio: A minister and a doctor who collected and wrote the stories and songs that began modern Frisian literature.

figures.name: Pieter Jelles Troelstra
figures.bio: A lawyer from Leeuwarden who led the Dutch socialists for thirty years and wrote much-loved verse in Frisian.

figures.name: Titus Brandsma
figures.bio: A farmer’s son from near Bolsward, Carmelite friar, professor and champion of the Frisian language. He opposed Nazi control of the press and died in Dachau. He was made a saint in 2022.

figures.name: Fedde Schurer
figures.bio: Poet and newspaper editor whose trial for criticising a judge set off the language riot of 1951.

figures.name: Atje Keulen-Deelstra
figures.bio: A farmer’s wife and mother of three who took up serious skating late and was four times world all-round champion.

figures.name: Sven Kramer
figures.bio: A skater from Heerenveen, nine times world all-round champion and winner of four Olympic gold medals.

history.detail: Farmers move onto the salt marshes of the north and soon begin to raise the first dwelling mounds.
The Frisians become tributaries of Rome. In AD 28 they revolt over a tax in ox hides and defeat a Roman force. The frontier is later fixed on the Rhine.
Under Aldgisl and Redbad the Frisians hold the coast from Flanders to the Weser and dominate North Sea trade from the port of Dorestad.
The Franks under Charles Martel defeat the Frisians and take their heartland. The missionary Boniface is killed at Dokkum in 754.
Charlemagne has the customs of the Frisians written down. Later legend credited him with granting their freedom.
Monasteries and farmers start to enclose the land with sea walls.
The Frisian lands govern themselves without feudal lords. Delegates of the sea-lands meet at the Upstalsboom near Aurich.
Count William IV of Holland lands with an army to conquer Friesland and is killed with most of his knights.
Worn down by feuds between two parties, Friesland falls to Duke Albert of Saxony. In 1524 it passes to the emperor Charles V.
Friesland is one of the seven United Provinces, with its own stadtholder at Leeuwarden and, from 1585, its own university at Franeker.
A society for Frisian language and literature is founded. The poems and tales of the Halbertsmas circulate widely.
Twenty-two skaters start, and nine finish.
Police with batons and water cannon break up a crowd outside the court in Leeuwarden. Frisian is admitted in court in 1956.
Frisian becomes a compulsory subject in primary schools in 1980. A law of 2014 confirms it as an official language of the province.

concepts.detail: The medieval condition of self-rule by free landowning farmers. It was justified by a legendary charter from Charlemagne and defended in several battles.
First the mounds, then the sea walls, then drainage by windmill and steam. The landscape is an artefact that needs constant upkeep.
Each holding maintained a section in proportion to its land, under inspection. The rule made cooperation a condition of ownership.
Villages are small and far apart, and clubs for sailing, skating, music and keatsen bind them. Things get done by joining in.
West Frisia in the Netherlands, East Frisia and the Saterland in Lower Saxony, and North Frisia in Schleswig-Holstein. They meet in a common council.
Almost all speakers are bilingual. The language is strong in speech and in the countryside and weaker in writing and in towns.
From Leeuwarden to tiny Sloten, which has some seven hundred inhabitants. In 2018 each was given a fountain by an international artist.
Bodies of landowners elected to manage dikes and water levels. They are older than the Dutch state and still levy their own tax.
A code of manners that values honesty, modesty and sobriety over polish.

facts.text: The Eleven Cities Tour has been held fifteen times since 1909. The ice must be at least fifteen centimetres thick along the whole route.
The Frisian flag was first described in the sixteenth century and officially adopted in 1957.
The black Friesian horse and the black-and-white Holstein Friesian cow both take their names from the region.
The Oera Linda Book, which claimed to be an ancient Frisian chronicle, appeared in 1867 and is a nineteenth-century hoax.
Old Frisian law lists three needs in which a mother may sell her child’s inheritance. One is when the child is naked and homeless in the dark mist and cold winter.
Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch governor of New Amsterdam, was the son of a Frisian minister.

sensitivity.note: Frisians are a living people and a recognised national minority in the Netherlands and Germany. This Onda was written from published sources, mostly about West Friesland, and Frisian readers are warmly invited to correct it.
requiredCaveats: North Frisia and East Frisia have their own histories, dialects and customs, which are touched on only lightly here.
The stubborn, silent Frisian is a stereotype that Frisians enjoy and also outgrow. Most live ordinary modern Dutch or German lives.
Several of the best-known sayings, including those of Grutte Pier and Gemme van Burmania, rest on tradition and were written down long after the event.
Pronunciations are approximate. Frisian has sounds that English spelling cannot show.
